title: Electromotive force (emf), internal resistance, and cells…
topicTitle: Electromotive force (emf), internal resistance, and cells in combination
notes: The emf of a cell is the work done per unit charge as charge is moved through the source. It is measured in volts. It is the open-circuit potential difference, when no current is drawn.
A real cell has internal resistance r. When current I flows, the terminal voltage is E − I r. The 'lost volts' I r heat the inside of the cell.

The current in a single loop is I = E / (R + r). A smaller external resistance draws a larger current and drops the terminal voltage further. Shorting a cell makes I = E/r, which can be large and damaging.
Two identical cells in series give emf 2E and internal resistance 2r, if they point the same way. The current in an external R is 2E / (R + 2r).
Two identical cells in parallel give emf E and internal resistance r/2. The parallel pair can supply a larger current before the terminal voltage sags, but the emf is still the emf of one cell.

Cells in opposition subtract their emfs. A 1.5 V cell set against a 1.5 V cell gives no net emf if they are identical, and a small difference of emf drives a current limited by both internal resistances.

universalFacts: Ohm's law: V = IR; R = ρL/A (resistivity ρ depends on material).
Series: R = ΣR; same I, voltages add. Parallel: 1/R = Σ1/R; same V, currents add.
Power P = VI = I²R = V²/R; internal resistance makes terminal V = E − Ir.

keyPoints: Emf is the energy per unit charge from the source.
Internal resistance is inside the cell.
Terminal voltage is less than emf when the cell supplies current.
Series cells add emfs. Parallel equal cells share current.
summary: Emf is the open-circuit voltage of a source. Internal resistance drops the terminal voltage to E − I r while the cell supplies current, and the loop current is E/(R+r). Identical cells in series add their emfs. Identical cells in parallel keep one emf and share the internal resistance.
